newsitem.title: USA: U.S. farm subsidy chief Grant Buntrock quits.
newsitem.headline: U.S. farm subsidy chief Grant Buntrock quits.

text.p: The head of the huge agency that gives out U.S. farm subsidies plans to resign in April, according to a letter the controversial chief gave to his staff that Reuters obtained on Wednesday.

"Now, it is, quite simply, time to move on as the Clinton Administration begins a new term with a new team," Grant Buntrock, administrator of the Farm Service Agency (FSA), said in a letter to employees dated Jan. 21.
In the letter, Buntrock said he would leave on April 4. He did not disclose what his next step would be.

News of his resignation came on the same day as a public meeting at his department's headquarters to discuss allegations of racial bias. The "public airing" followed a series of regional meetings on the issue.

His department has been at the centre of recent complaints about racial bias, with black farmers contending they have long endured discrimination in lending programmes and that racism was the basis for loan rejections and foreclosures.
Agriculture Secretary Dan Glickman ordered a halt in foreclosure sales last month and announced a wide-ranging civil rights review at the department.
"We recognise there have been instances of discrimination in responding to requests for our services in the past, and we deplore it," Buntrock told the Washington Post in December.

His resignation follows other high-profile departures. Four of the six undersecretaries have resigned in the past three months at the department. Glickman hopes to begin filling the posts by the end of the month.

As FSA head, Buntrock was in charge of federal farm subsidies, crop insurance, the 36.4 million-acre Conservation Reserve, and farm ownership and operating loan programmes. The agency has nearly 20,000 workers at a web of offices located in nearly every county.

During his tenure as FSA chief, Buntrock was named in a Justice Department investigation of improper political fund-raising at the Agriculture Department in support of President Bill Clinton's election in 1992.
Four men involved in illegal political fund-raising at the agriculture department were sentenced last month to two years probation and ordered to pay modest fines.
The Justice Department investigation said Buntrock had met in 1992 with four mid-level Agriculture Department supervisors who later solicited campaign donations from co-workers.
At that time, Buntrock worked for a farmers' group and was helping to raise funds for Farmers and Ranchers '92, a political action committee that backed Clinton.
Buntrock strongly denied any wrongdoing and said political affiliation played no role in job assignments during his tenure.
